course.title: Liver
course.html:
Anatomy

  • Surgical anatomy is different from classical anatomy → Cuinauds division of liver in 8 segments
  • Division based on hepatic veins and portal branches
  • Surgical lobes divided by Cantlie’s line, portal fissure or main scizura
  • Vena cava inferior and gallbladder bed → first division in surgical right and left liver lobe
  • Next division is into 4 sectors that are separated by scissurae containing three main hepatic veins
  • Main scissura contains middle hepatic vein
  • Right liver divided into anterior sector (segments V and VIII) and posterior sector (segments VI and VII) by right scissura (right hepatic vein)
  • Left hepatic vein divides into segments IV and II + III
  • Finally subdivision of sectors by portal vein → leads to segments which have single portal triad (pedicle) (portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct)
  • Portal vein = superior + inferior mesenteric + splenic vein
  • Provides 75% of blood supply → richer in oxigen
  • Explains possibility of maintaining hepatic function after arterial ligation or embolization
  • Common hepatic artery comes from celiac axis → gives gastroduodenal artery and continues as proper hepatic artery in pedicle (anterior to vena porta and left of main bile duct)
  • Cystic artery originates from right or proper hepatic artery
  • Hepatic veins - right, middle and left
  • Peritoneal duplications on liver surface are mistakenly named ligaments
  • First step of any major liver surgery is mobilization of liver by transecting these ligaments
  • Diaphragmatic peritoneal duplications - coronary ligament → continue at right and left triangular ligaments
  • Falciform ligament connects liver to diaphragm and abd. wall; limit between left and right anatomic lobe
  • Ligamentum teres/ round ligament (obliterated umbilical vein) in inferior part of falciform ligament
  • Runs from umbilicus to umbilical fissure on inferior surface of liver
  • Umbilical fissure contains left portal triad

Benign liver diseases

Simple cyst

= serous, biliary, non-parasitic cyst lined by biliary-type epithelium; result from progressive dilation of biliary microhamartomas

  • Contain fluids identical to plasma secreted by epithelium → aspiration of fluid does not lead to resolution
  • No malignant transformation
  • No communication with biliary tree
  • Usually asymptomatic
  • Symptoms are non-specific and usually compressive in large volume cysts
  • Diagnosis by US
  • If complicated by hemorrhage → DD neoplastic cyst → elevated CA 19.9 level in aspirated fluid
  • Multicystic disease = adult polycystic liver disease (congenital) → rupture, hemorrhage, infection and liver failure
  • Surgical (laparoscopic) treatment only in symptomatic cases !
  • After aspiration and inspection of sclerosing liquid → resection of superficialized cysts wall (unroofing)
  • cavity inspected with telescope
  • If aspirated liquid contains blood or mucus → cytology mandatory

Bile duct cyst

Classification

Complications

  • Lithiasis
  • Cholangitis
  • Malignant degeneration

Treatment

  • Resection → if necessary with hepatectomy and bilio-jejunostomy on Y loop

Traumatic cyst

  • Posttraumatic intrahepatic liquid collections
  • Lesion of biliary and/or vascular structures after blunt abdominal traumas
  • Lacking epithelium, collection is not a real cyst
  • Some may remain asymptomatic
  • If symptomatic or complicated (infection, hemobilia) → treatment
  • Minimally invasive approach with interventional angiography (embolisation of affected artery) and/ or ERCP (+/- ES)

Portal hypertension

= hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) of ≥ 6mmHg

  • HVPG > 10mmHg is clinically significant
  • - HVPG = pressure gradient between WHVP and FHPV; pressure gradient between portal vein + IVC
  • Porto-caval anastomosis is affected → shunting of blood → dilation and even rupture of collateral circulation
    • upper gastric and lower esophageal veins → esophageal varices
caput medusa
secondary hemorrhoids

Causes

Pre-hepatic- Portal vein thrombosis
HepaticHepatic- Cirrhosis = most common cause
- Mostly due to hepatitis B, C; alcohol
Post-hepatic- Budd Chiari syndrome (occlusion of hepatic veins)

Diagnostics

US- Cavernous transformation of portal vein
- Portal vein dilated to > 13 mm (normal < 13mm)
- SV and SMV diameter ↑ (normal < 10mm)
- Lack of respiratory variation of SV and SMV (normal ≥ 40%)
- ↑ blood flow via portosystemic anastomoses using duplex
- ↑ spleen size (normal < 12cm; < 45cm²)
- Presence of porto-systemic collaterals
- Presence of ascites
Abdominal CT- Portal vein thrombosis
Esophago-gastro-
duodenoscopy		- Assessment and treatment of esophageal varices

Prevention of recurrent hemorrhage

  • 1. Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS)
    • Minimal invasive
    • Establishing intrahepatic communication between hepatic vein and branch of portal vein
    • Under US guidance → catheter inserted in right internal jugular vein → inferior vena cava → right hepatic vein → angulated needle inserted until portal vein branch → titanium wire stent left in place
    • TIPSS applied for emergency treatment of hemorrhage from esophageal varices
    • Good method to gain time till matching liver can be transplanted
Other indications for TIPSSContraindications for TIPSS
- Refractory ascites and/or hydrothorax
- Patients contraindicated for surgical shunt
- Budd-Chiari syndrome		- Liver failure
- Advanced cardiac disease
- Active peritoneal, intrahepatic, or systemic infections
- Hepatic tumors likely to be intercepted during procedure
2. Portosystemic shunts
Nonselective= are abandoned because volume of portal blood unprocessed by liver drained directly in
systemic flow is too large
Selective- Like spleno-renal shunt
- Disadvantage = losing their efficiency in few years
→ This happens as peripancreatic veins dilate and bring increased blood flow to submucosal
varicose veins with recurrent hemorrhage
Partial- best partial shunt consists in portocaval anastomosis with interposition of calibrated 8-9 mm
teflon graft
- If larger there is important risk of encephalopathy
- If smaller thrombosis will inactivate shunt
  • 3. Hepatic transplantation
Liver abscess
Routes of bacterial spread to liver- Biliary tree
- Portal vein
- Hepatic artery
- Direct extension of nearby focus of infection
- Trauma
- Cryptogenic (microinfarction)
Microorganisms involved- E. coli
- Klebsiella
- Enterococcus
+ Bacteroides and streptococcal species
  • Due to course of right portal branch (runs almost straight) → seeding of right lobe more frequent

Causes of ascending cholangitis

  • CBD lithiasis or other obstructions
  • Intrahepatic stones (more common in Asia)
  • Malignant obstruction (usually after ERCP or stenting)
  • Caroli’s disease
  • Stenotic bilio-enteric anastomosis

Clinical

  • Fever, chills
  • RUQ pain, tenderness
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Malaise
  • Jaundice → preexisting biliary disease or liver failure
  • Secondary peritonitis after rupture is quite rare
  • If situated on upper surface of liver → abscess can cause reactive pleural collection

Lab

  • Leukocytosis, CRP and ESR high
  • Altered liver function tests
  • Anemia
  • Hypoalbuminemia
  • Cultures (+ anaerobic, fungi) from puncture are mandatory

Imaging

  • US can detect > 90% of the cases
  • CT offers better results in areas blocked by inferior lungs and in small abscesses, can identify initial lesion
  • Both allow guidance of percutaneous punction and drainage

DD

  • Amoebic abscess
  • Echinococcal Garbi IV cyst

Treatment

Medical- Broad-spectrum AB covering gram negative and positive
SurgicalSurgical- Laparoscopic
- Must be considered if percutaneous drainage is contraindicated or unsuccessful

Amebic liver abscess

  • Caused by Entamoeba histolytica
  • More frequently in right lobe
  • Mainly males affected
  • Via contaminated water, food or humans → gets into portal flow → liver → produces necrosis
  • Symptoms are same as for liver abscess ++ diarrhea and recent travel !

Treatment

  • Nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, secnidazole, tinidazole)
  • Chloroquine
  • Iodoquinol
  • Dehydroeme
  • Paromomycin
  • Diloxanide furoate
Benign liver tumors
Liver cell adenoma (LCA)= proliferation of hepatocytes
- Rest of liver unchanged
- Women with prolonged use of oral contraceptives
- Oral contraceptives have to be stopped
- Mostly singular
- Adenomatosis if over 10
- Consists of cords of benign hepatocytes, reduced fibrous tissue and small vessels
with rich arterial supply (explains risk of bleeding)
- Rupture with intraperitoneal bleeding (increased risk in pregnancy and subcapsular)
- Malignant transformation not demonstrated but postulated
- Resection advisable
Focal nodular hyperplasia
(FNH)		= second most common benign solid tumor of liver
- Central scar and artery, cords of hepatocytes divided by fibrous tracts
- Percutaneous biopsy possible but not always of help
- Affects young women
- Use of oral contraceptives
- Majority asymptomatic
- Rarely large
- Surgery if symptomatic
Hemangioma (H)= most common benign tumor of liver
- Affects more frequently women
- Congenital vascular malformation
- No risk of malignant degeneration
  • Complicated by rupture, superinfection
  • Can lead to Kasbach-Merritt syndrome (thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy

secondary to thrombosis)

  • In children large H can act as arteriovenous shunt and lead to heart failure
  • US can raise suspicion
  • MRI - typical peripheral nodular enhancement
  • Biopsy contraindicated !!! (very high risk of bleeding)
  • In symptomatic and complicated cases → surgery with Pringle maneuver
  • CyberKnife system combines robotics and tridimensional liver reconstruction to

focus beams of radiation on tumor

Diagnosis

  • 1. Detection usually by ultrasound
  • 2. If suspect mass dynamic CT scan
  • 3. If lesion with uniform contrast enhancement on CT scan without aspect of hemangiomas, viral hepatitis markers

and tumor markers (AFP, CEA) to rule out hepatocellular carcinoma and colorectal metastasis

  • 4. If still unclear MRI in selected cases with angiography
  • 5. If HCC possible biopsy
Treatment indication for benign tumorsTreatment types
- Symptomatic
- Complicated
- Suspect of malignant degeneration
- Very large
- Fast growing		- Enucleation (tumorectomy)
- Atypical resection
- Segmentectomy
- Bisegmentectomy or other major resection
- Transplantation (exceptionally)
- Embolization (selective)
- Ablation (several types)
→ Always remove in a tissue sparing manner

Hydatid cyst

= zoonotic infection caused by tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus causing cystic echinococcosis (CE)

  • Ingestion of food, water or dirty hands contaminated by eggs in feces of definitive host (dog, jackal or carnivore)
  • Cyst is surrounded by inflammatory tissue = pericyst

Organs affected

  • Liver
  • Lung
  • Other organs: spleen, brain, bones, eye

Symptoms caused by

  • Rupture of cyst
  • Infection of cyst or affected organs
  • Compression of any neighbouring organ

Rupture of liver cyst can happen in

  • Biliary tree
  • Free peritoneum
  • Surrounding hollow viscus
  • Erosion into biliary tree = cysto-biliary fistula
  • Causes allergic symptoms: flushing, urticaria, major rupture frequently leads to anaphylactic shock (protein in

fluid)

  • Pain, fever, jaundice, asymmetric hepatomegaly in angiocolitis
  • Infection of cavity, with symptoms of hepatic abscess
  • Biliary obstruction by late stenosis of Oddi sphincter due to irritating hydatid liquid
  • Depending on affected organ → content of cyst can be eliminated by vomit, stool or urine
  • Cysts close to inferior surface of liver → open in free peritoneum with long-term risk of hydatidosis (peritoneal seeding of

scolex, with multiple cysts developing)

  • Cysts on upper surface of liver → perforate diaphragm but seldomly open in free pleural cavity

DD

SyndromesDiseases
- Jaundice
- Persistent fever
- Hepatomegaly
- Allergic reaction		- Biliary obstruction
- Acute hepatitis
- Hepatic abscesses
- Hepatic nonparasitic cyst
- Budd-Chiari Syndrome
- Hepatic tumors, primary and metastatic

Lab

  • ↑ Bilirubin, ALP, leukocytosis → biliary obstruction
  • Eosinophilia → allergic reaction
  • ELISA test = most reliable, 90% sensitivity
  • Casoni test no longer used

Imaging

  • Plain abdominal X-ray is usually normal, seldom calcifications
  • US = best method for diagnosis
  • Intraoperative US
  • CT and MRI (not routinely used)
  • ERCP - more useful in biliary complicated cysts, method of choice for diagnose and minimally invasive treatment

(sphincterothomy and membrane extraction)

Gharbi´s Classification

II: hydatic sand

III: daughter cysts

  • If no daughter cysts, hydatid sand or membranes = Gharbi I → DD to non-parasitic cyst is difficult
  • The parasites are dead when infection or calcification occurs

Treatment

  • ERCP in cysto-biliary fistulae
  • Chemotherapy alone has limited indications (contraindication of surgery, many cysts, more than one organ affected)
  • useless in complicated and dead cysts
  • Given in combination with another treatment -> Albendazole, mebendazole for 3-6 month
  • PAIR (puncture, aspiration, scolicidal agent injection, re-aspiration after 15 min.) = US guided technique
  • cavity may be repeatedly washed in same session and is left filled with isotonic saline solution
  • presence of scolices in aspirated liquid confirmes diagnosis
  • PAIR can be applied in some contraindications of surgery, but has to be avoided in Gharbi IV and complicated,

superficial (spillage and seeding risk) cysts

  • Surgery indicated in most cases -> best option
Total pericystectomy- Consists in removing parasite together with whole pericyst
- Hemorrhage risks higher but postoperative outcome is better (complications
associated to residual cavity (biliary fistulae, abscess) are eliminated)
Hepatic resection- Avoids risk of seeding but may be too aggressive as it removes also healthy tissue
- Applied in large cysts when only small part of peripheral liver has to be sacrificed
Cystectomy with partial- Removes parasite with area of pericyst that is superficial
pericystectomy
MarsupialisationMarsupialisation- Suturing edges of pericyst to abdominal wall -> opening cyst and draining it
through skin
- Obsolete technique

Main objectives of surgical treatment

  • Sterilization of parasite by injecting scolicidal substance
  • Removal of inactivated parasite
  • Reduction of residual cavity

Prophylaxis

  • Proper hands hygiene
  • Correct food processing for humans
  • Proper handling of herbivores feces
  • Dealing with problem of rogue dogs
  • Medical prophilaxy of echinococcosis in dogs
  • Correct food processing for dogs

Malignant liver lesions

Anatomical liver resection for liver metastasis

  • → Couinaud classification
Most common
nomenclature		SynonymRemoved segments
Right hepatectomyRight hepatic lobectomyV, VI, VII, VIII
Extended rightExtended right hepatic lobectomy, right trisegmentectomyIV, V, VI, VII, VIII
hepatectomy
Left hepatectomyLeft hepatic lobectomyII, III, IV
Extended leftExtended left hepatic lobectomy, left trisegmentectomyII, III, IV, V, VIII
hepatectomy
Left lateralLeft lobectomy, bisegmentectomyII, III
segmentectomy
Lobectomy
  • Evaluation of liver tumors starts with ultrasound
  • In metastasis -> local recurrence of primary cancer has to be excluded by colonoscopy and CT
  • Chest x-ray to exclude concomitent pulmonary metastasis
  • CT volumetric analysis necessary for assessment of adequate residual liver volume
  • Must be correlated with function, Child-Pugh classification being widely used for cirrhosis
  • Under normal conditions 20%/ 30% of residual volume sufficient, in cirrhosis at least 40%
  • Principle in resection of liver tumors -> spare parenchyma -> only 1 cm safety margin
  • Number, position and relation to major vessels must be accurately established by CT portography
  • Invasion in major hepatic elements or IVC is not contraindication for surgery
  • Laparoscopic ultrasound allows thorough assessment
  • Intraoperatively bleeding and biliary leaks = major problem and postoperative causes for morbidity
  • Resection in small tumors - wedge resections and non-anatomical resections (tumorectomies)
  • Inflow control to check correct segmental margins -> corresponding portal branch clampt -> change in color of parenchyma delineates resection
  • Pringle maneuver – to prevent hemorrhage -> clamps placed on IVC above and below liver for max. 40 min (better 20 min + 5-10 min. break)
  • Another method to minimize bleeding -> low CVP
  • Adjuvant regional chemotherapy - placing catheter in proper hepatic artery
  • Liver transplantation recommended in primary liver tumors (not in secondary malignancies)

Primary hepatic carcinoma (HCC)

Etiology

  • Cirrhosis (80%)
    • Alcohol (1/3 of HCC)
    • Hepatitis B, C
    • Hemochromatosis
    • Wilson’s
    • Tyrosinemia
    • Glycogen storage disease
    • Aflatoxin
Signs and symptoms
(similar to cirrhosis)		- Hepatomegaly
- Jaundice
- Collateral venous circulation (esophageal varices, hemorrhoids, caput
medusae etc.)
- Variceal bleeding
- Splenomegaly
- Spider angiomata
- Flapping tremor and hepatic encephalopathy
- Ascites
- Weight loss - cachexia
Lab- Usual modified liver values in cirrhosis
- Alpha-fetoprotein > 20ng/ml (values > 500ng/ml = specific for HCC)
Imaging- US (fist choice & screening)
- CT
- MRI = best method
→ Tumoral invasion in portal branch is characteristic for HCC
- Angiography may show tumors < 1cm
- Biopsy caries risk of tumoral seeding and bleeding

Medical care must be recommended considering certain criteria

  • Size, number
  • Location
  • Presence of cirrhosis
  • Patency of portal vein
  • Metastatic disease

Treatment

  • Relatively chemotherapy-resistant tumor -> systemic chemotherapy + immunomodulators (interferon-alpha) to

achieve responds

  • Anti-angiogenesis agents (bevacizumab) → inhibiting neovascular formation
  • Chemoembolization
  • In selected cases liver resection is possible
  • Operative risk must be considered by combining data on class of cirrhosis, comorbidities, overall health status
  • Unfortunately, HCC develops on cirrhotic liver and is usually multicentric
  • Fibrolamellar HCC has better prognosis for survival after surgical resection
  • Liver transplantation in HCC is advisable if local extent is limited
  • When surgery is contraindicated tumor ablation can be of help

Cholangiocarcinoma

= malignancies of biliary duct system

  • Can be located intrahepatic, perihilar, extrahepatic

S. biliary chapter

Metastatic tumors of liver

  • Usually multiple
  • Metastatic sites is not contraindication for surgical treatment anymore, but not all provide increased survival
  • Colo-rectal metastasis always increases 5-year survival
  • Synchronous liver metastasis resected in single procedure with primary colo-rectal tumor if feasible

Most frequent origins

  • Melanoma
  • Pancreas
  • Colon and rectum
  • But any digestive tumor can lead to liver mets !

Treatment

  • Percutaneous ethanol or acetic acid injection (abandoned)
  • Cryotherapy (placed laparoscopically or under US guidance)
  • Radiofrequency ablation (fast vibration of ions) -> rises temp. and coagulates proteins BUT only radius of 3 cm
    • Saline-enhanced radiofrequency ablation (Tissuelink RM) -> increases radius to 5 cm
    • Circulating blood in large vessels has cooling effect -> weaker effect in close proximity
    • Complications: hemorrhage and hematoma, abscess, thrombosis, biliary duct stenosis
  • Microwaves (rotation and vibration of water molecules with heat production)
  • High intensity focused US (HIFU) -> US produces heat -> coagulation with necrosis
  • CyberKnife (combines robotics and tridimensional liver reconstruction to focus beams of radiation on tumor)
  • Surgical resection with safety margins (1cm) !
  • Procedures can be combined depending on accessibility of mets (e.g., resection + ablation)

Outcome in metastatic tumors -> negative predictive factors

  • Lymph node involvement
  • Multiple metastasis
  • Tumor > 5 cm
  • If metachronous metastasis are diagnosed in less than a year
  • CEA > 200 ng/ml preoperatively

Neoplastic cyst

  • Cystadenoma = premalignant lesion → can degenerate into cystadenocarcinoma
  • Very rare
  • More frequently in women > 40 y.
  • Irregular spheroidal surface, septated with polypoid or papillary projections
  • Wall thickened with more solid or even calcified parts
  • Fluid inside must be aspirated and processed (mucus, CA 19-9, cytology)
mucinous
cystectomy
  • Cystadenocarcinoma resected with safety margin

book.html:
The liver

Ion Cosmin Puia

BENIGN LIVER DISORDERS

Anatomy

The first hepatectomy was performed by Berta in 1716, who removed a piece of eviscerated liver. At the beginning of the 20th century suturing major hepatic vessels and the use of cautery for small vessels brought the first successful liver operations. Pringle, in 1908, used the digital compression of the liver pedicle for temporary hemostasis. The first anatomic liver resection was performed by Lortat-Jacob in 1952 in France. The segmental anatomy of the liver described by Couinaud represented the anatomic basis of liver surgery.

Surgical anatomy is quite different from the classical anatomy of the liver. The surgical lobes are divided by Cantlie’s line, portal fissure or main scizura. This is a plane defined by the left side of vena cava inferior (VCIhollow vein) and the gallbladder bed. The first division is in the right and left portal branch, corresponding to the right and left liver (or surgical lobe). The right pedicle has a short extrahepatic segment but the left follows a long extrahepatic course and is hence easier to dissect. The surgical importance lies also in the possibility to widen a bilio-jejunal anastomosis by lengthening the incision on the main bile duct towards the left branch. The next division is into four sectors that are separated by scissurae containing the three main hepatic veins.

The main scissura contains the middle hepatic vein. The right liver is divided into an anterior sector (segments V and VIII) and a posterior sector (segments VI and VII) by the right scissura that contains the right hepatic vein. Finally the subdivision of the sectors leads to segments which have a single portal triad (pedicle) composed of a portal vein, hepatic artery and a bile duct.

The portal vein is formed posterior to the pancreas from the confluence of the mesenteric and the splenic vein. It provides roughly 75% of the liver’s blood supply and is much richer in oxigen than usual venous blood. This explains the possibility of maintaining the hepatic function after arterial ligation or embolization. It is the most posterior element of the hepatic pedicle.

The hepatic artery is one or the three branches of the celiac axis. Initially named common hepatic artery it gives the gastroduodenal artery and continues as the proper hepatic artery in the pedicle, where it is anterior to the vena porta and to the left of the main bile duct. The cystic artery originates from the right or proper hepatic artery.

The hepatic veins are the right, middle and left. Usually the middle and left unite and, unlike the right one, have no extraparenchymal segment. Broadly speaking the right veins is flanked by segments VI, VII and V, VIII, the middle by V, VIII and IV and the lateral by IV and II, III. Segment I or Spiegel lobe lies in close contact to the VCI and has its own veins that drain directly into the VCI.

The peritoneal duplications on the liver surface are mistakenly named ligaments. The first step of any major liver surgery is the correct mobilization of the liver by transecting these ligaments. The diaphragmatic peritoneal duplications are the coronary ligament and continue at their extremities with the right and left triangular ligaments. The falciform ligament connects the liver to the diaphragm and abdominal wall. Ligamentum teres (the obliterated umbilical vein) is in the inferior part of the falciform ligament. It runs from the umbilicus to the umbilical fissure, on the inferior surface of the liver. The umbilical fissure contains the left portal triad. The falciform ligament is the limit between the left and right anatomic lobe.

SIMPLE CYSTS

Simple (serous, biliary, non-parasitic) cysts are lined by biliary-type epithelium and may result from progressive dilatation of biliary microhamartomas. A malignant transformation is impossible. They do not communicate with the biliary tree. The liquid has a composition identical to plasma and is secreted by the epithelium. This is why a simple aspiration without destruction of the secreting epithelium results in recurrency.

Usually asymptomatic, they affect 5% of the population, but no more than 10-15% of these patients have symptoms. These are non-specific and linked to the volume and compression of the cysts.

Complications are exceptional.

Diagnose is usually made by ultrasound which should suffice for the differential. An exception are hydatid cysts type Gharbi I, when an ELISA test may be necessary.

If complicated by a hemorrhage, imaging may have difficulties in differentiating from a neoplastic cyst. If the aspirated liquid has an elevated CA19-9 level the cyst may be neoplastic. If it contains scolices it is a hydatid cyst.

Prior to the injection of a sclerosing substance a communication with the biliary tree must be excluded (risk of sclerosing cholangitis) by injecting iodinated contrast.

The multicystic disease is different from the adult polycystic liver disease

which is congenital and associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. The complications (rupture, hemorrhage, infection and liver failure) are rare.

Surgical treatment, preferable by laparoscopic approach, is indicated only in symptomatic cases. After aspiration and inspection of the liquid the-next step is the wide resection of the superficialised cysts wall (unroofing), which is the technique of choice. The cavity can be inspected with the telescope. The secretion will be absorbed by the peritoneum.

If the aspirated liquid contains blood or mucus cytology is mandatory. The resected cystic wall must be processed in frozen and permanent sections, especially if papillary outgrowths are present on the inner surface.

BILE DUCT CYSTS

Type IV bile duct cysts are located on both the extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts. Caroli’s disease (type V) is defined by multiple intrahepatic cysts located more frecquently on the left surgical lobe. The complications of the bile duct cysts are lithiasis, cholangitis and malignant degeneration. The treatment is resection, if necessary with hepatectomy, and bilio-jejunostomy on “Y” loop. Diffuse advanced forms can benefit from transplantation.

NEOPLASTIC CYSTS

Cystadenoma is a premalignant lesion which can degenerate into a cystadenocarcinoma. Very rare, it is diagnosed more frequently in women older than the age of 40. The cyst has an irregular spheroidal surface, is septated with polypoid or papillary projections.

The wall is thickened with more solid or even calcified parts. The fluid contained in these cysts must be aspirated and processed (mucus, CA19-9, cytology). A hemorrhagic or mucinous aspect must arouse suspicion. Frozen sections may help.

Cystadenoma may be removed by cystectomy but cystadenocarcinoma must be resected with a safety margin. If the permanent histologic diagnose is cystadenocarcinoma and only unroofing was done, reoperation with liver resection is mandatory.

TRAUMATIC CYSTS

Posttraumatic intrahepatic liquid collections are the consequence of blunt abdominal traumas. The lesion of the biliary and/or vascular structures lead to the intraparenchymal accumulation of liquid. Lacking a epithelium the collection is not really a cyst. Some may remain asymptomatic. If symptomatic or complicated (infection, hemobilia) the treatment can combine a minimally invasive approach with interventional angiography (embolisation of the affected artery) and or ERCP (+/- ES).

PORTAL HYPERTENSION

Cirrhosis of the liver is by far the first cause of portal hypertension. Cirrhosis is defined by fibrosis and chaotic nodular regeneration, both of them altering the tridimensional architecture of the liver. Theses changes lead to an increased resistance to the passage of the portal blood flow, the portal hypertension.

The most common causes of cirrhosis are alcoholism and hepatitis B and C.

There are a number of connections between the portal venous system and the systemic venous system. The impaired portal flow finds passage through these connections. The high pressure leads to their dilation and rupture. These anasthomosis are:

  • the upper gastric and lower esophageal veins, leading to esophageal varices, the main cause for upper gastroesophageal bleeding
  • recanalised umbilical vein and abdominal wall veins, which give the head of the medusa around the umbilicus
  • superior, medium and inferior rectal veins, which dilate to form secondary hemorrhoids, a source of inferior gastrointestinal bleeding.

Durable prevention of recurrent hemorrhage from esophageal varices can be obtained by :

-transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt ( TIPSS)

-portosystemic shunts

-hepatic transplantation.

TIPSS is a minimally invasive technique consisting in establishing an intrahepatic communication between a hepatic vein and a branch of the portal vein. Other indications for TIPSS are:

- refractory ascites and/or hydrothorax

- patients contraindicated for surgical shunt

- Budd-Chiari syndrome.

Contraindications for TIPSS are:

- liver failure

- advanced cardiac disease

- active peritoneal, intrahepatic, or systemic infections

- hepatic tumors likely to be intercepted during the procedure.

Under ultrasound guidance a catheter is inserted in the right internal jugular vein. The progression to the inferior vena cava and (usually right) hepatic vein is followed on the screen. An angled guiding catheter is used for several dilating sheaths. An angulated needle is then inserted and advanced until a portal vein branch is reached. Needle passes are generally "blind" or ultrasound guidance can be used. The correct position is confirmed by injecting iodinated contrast media and a portal venogram is obtained. A stiff guidewire and an angioplasty balloon are used to dilate the vein walls and parenchymal tract (between hepatic vein and portal vein). A self expanding titanium wire stent is left in place thus permitting the decompression of the portal hypertension.

TIPSS can be applied, unlike portosystemic shunts, for the emergency treatment of the hemorrhage from esophageal varices. It is a good method to gain time till a matching liver can be transplanted because after a variable period it will be obstructed by thrombose. Unfortunately the durable desobstruction can seldom be achieved. If the caliber of the shunt is too large and the patient develops encefalopathy a reduction can be slipped in place by the same interventional radiology methods.

Portosystemic shunts can be classified as nonselective, selective, or partial.

Nonselective shunts were abandoned because the volume of portal blood unprocessed by the liver drained directly in the systemic flow is too large. Substances acting like neurotransmitters and toxins reach the brain and produce hepatic encephalopathy.

Selective shunts, like the spleno-renal shunt, have the disadvantage of losing their efficiency in a few years. This happens as the peripancreatic veins dilate and bring an increased bloodflow to the submucosal varicose veins, with recurrent hemorrhage.

The best partial shunt consists in a portocaval anasthomosis with interposition of a calibrated 8-9 mm teflon graft. If larger there is an important risk of encephalopathy. If smaller thrombosis will inactivate the shunt.

LIVER ABSCESSES

Ochsner and DeBakey published in 1938 a classic paper on pyogenic liver abscesses. In the preantibiotic era pyogenic liver abscesses were secondary to acute appendicitis and affected young adults.

Although the liver has a high clearance capacity for bacteria brought by the portal flow this may be submerged in several situations.

The routes of bacterial spread to the liver include:

- biliary tree most common (due to ascending Cholangitis)

- portal vein

- hepatic artery

- direct extension of a nearby focus of infection

- trauma

- cryptogenic.

Organisms most commonly involved in pyogenic liver abscess are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Enterococcus. Bacteroides and Streptococcal species are alsofound.

Ascending cholangitis may be caused by:

- common bile duct lithiasis or other obstructions

- intrahepatic stones ( more frequent in SE Asia)

Any infections of the territory drained by the portal vein can cause infectious pylephlebitis and subsequently deliver bacteria to the liver.

During septicemia the arterial flow inoculates bacteria into the liver.

Direct inoculation into a healthy liver from a contiguous abscess is uncommon.

In trauma an area of necrotic liver can develop into an abscess. Other hepatic necrosis like the ablative procedures can evolve in a similar way.

Cryptogenic abscesses could be explained by microembolism or microinfarction, areas infected by the hematogenous way.

Due to course of the right portal branch which runs almost straight, the seeding of the right lobe is more frequent.

Solitary abscesses can be encountered in about 50%.

At abdominal exploration, hepatic abscesses are fluctuant to palpation, but deeper abscesses may not be visible and can be difficult to feel.

Patients usually present with chills, fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tenderness and malaise. Peritonitis secondary to rupture is rare because the area imminent for rupture is usually blocked by the surrounding viscera. Tenderness and hepatomegalia can be found. Jaundice can be explained by the preexisting biliary disease or by liver failure. If situated on the upper, convex surface of the liver the abscess can cause a reactive pleural collection.

Nonspecific abnormalities of blood tests are common in pyogenic abscesses. Leukocytosis and altered liver function tests are due to the acute character and location of the abscess. Anemia, hypoalbuminemia or other markers of a hepatoprive syndrome indicate a more chronic aspect of the evolution.

Ultrasound can detect > 90% of the cases. CT offers better results in areas blocked by the inferior part of the lungs and in small abscesses and can identify the initial lesion (appendicitis, CBD lithiasis , diverticulitis).

The differential from amoebic abscess or echinococcal Garbi IV cyst only on imaging may need serological testing as a back-up. Punction and therapeutic antibiotic test may be also helpful.

The advent of ultrasound and CT allowed a better guidance of the percutaneous punction and drainage of the abscesses. Cultures from the obtained pus on standard and special media (anaerobic, fungi) are mandatory.

Antibiotic treatment must precede punction or surgery but has to be adapted to antibiogram. Broad-spectrum antibiotic combinations covering gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria and anaerobes are the rule.

Surgical treatment, preferably with a laparoscopic approach, must be considered if percutaneous treatment is contraindicated or unsuccessful.

Especially multiple abscesses had a very high mortality rate until the advent of efficient antibiotics (imipenem ).

AMEBIC LIVER ABSCESS

The amebic liver abscess is caused by Entamoeba histolytica and similar to the piogenic abscess affects more frequently the right lobe. The sex ratio male: female is 10:1.

The trophozoit from contamined water, food or humans gets into the portal flow, reaches the liver and produces a necrosis which can be bacterially superinfected.

The symptoms and signs do not differ from a liver abscess. Diarrhea and a recent travel to an endemic area can orientate diagnose.

The specific treatment for amoebic abscess can be:

- nitroimidazoles (metronidazole, secnidazole, tinidazole)

- chloroquine,

- iodoquinol

- dehydroeme

- paromomycin

- diloxanide furoate

BENIGN LIVER LESIONS

The benign liver lesions can be solid or cystic. Most of them are asymptomatic and are discovered with higher frequency due to an easier access to better imaging techniques.

Solid benign tumors are, in order of increasing frequency:

- liver cell adenoma ( LCA)

- focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH)

- hemangioma (H).

The rationale steps for diagnose can be:

1. detection usually by ultrasound

2. if suspect mass dynamic CT scan

3. if lesion with uniform enhancement with contrast on CT scan

without aspect of hemangiomas,viral hepatitis markers and tumor

markers (AFP, CEA) to rule out hepatocellular carcinoma and colo-

rectal metastasis

4. if still unclear MRI , in selected cases with angiography

5. if HCC possible biopsy.

The treatment is indicated if the benign tumor is:

- symptomatic

- complicated

- suspect of malignant degeneration

- very large

- fast growing. Types of treatment:

  • enucleation (tumorectomy)
  • atypical resection
  • segmentectomy
  • bisegmentectomy or other major resection
  • transplantation (exceptionally)
  • embolization (selective)
  • ablation (several types).

In benign lesions the tumor has to be removed in a tissue-sparing manner. Liver cell adenoma (LCA) has following features:

  • it is a proliferation of hepatocytes
  • rest of the liver unchanged
  • women with prolonged use of oral contraceptives
  • oral contraceptives have to be stopped
  • mostly singular
  • adenomatosis if over 10
  • consists of cords of benign hepatocytes, reduced fibrous tissue and small vessels with rich arterial supply (explains the risk of bleeding)
  • rupture with intraperitoneal bleeding (increased risk in pregnancy and subcapsular)
  • malignant transformation not demonstrated but postulated
  • resection advisable.

Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) has following characteristics:

  • second most common benign solid tumor of the liver
  • central scar and artery, cords of hepatocytes divided by fibrous tracts
  • percutaneous biopsy possible but not always of help
  • affects young women
  • use of oral contraceptives
  • majority asymptomatic
  • rarely large
  • surgery if symptomatic.

Hemangioma has certain characteristics:

  • most common benign tumor of the liver
  • affects more frequently women
  • supposed to be a congenital vascular malformation
  • no risk of malignant degeneration
  • complicated by rupture, superinfection
  • can lead to Kasbach-Merritt syndrome ( thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy secondary to thrombosis)
  • in children large H can act as an arteriovenous shunt and lead to heart failure
  • ultrasound can raise suspicion of H
  • MRI - typical peripheral nodular enhancement
  • Isotopic labeled red blood cell scans used before MRI was available
  • Biopsy contraindicated
  • In symptomatic and complicated cases surgery with Pringle maneuver advisable.
  • prior to transaction the liver parenchyma as the effect is better if a thin layer of liquid intermediates the contact between the electrode and the tissue.
  • CyberKnife system combines robotics and tridimensional liver reconstruction to focus beams of radiation on the tumor.

LIVER TRAUMA

  • The liver is the largest parenchymal abdominal organ and is only partially

protected by the right hypochondrium and is affected by both penetrating (stab and gunshot wounds) and blunt trauma. The first coherent classification combining the degree of lesion with the recommended repair was established by Aldrete in 1979. Although some recommendations became obsolete due to new means of hemostasis, it is still in use:

  • I. Small lacerations with minimal bleeding. Usually in type I lesions

bleeding has ceased at laparotomy. Drainage is sufficient.

  • II. Moderate lacerations with active and significant bleeding. The means

of obtaining hemostasis may be: compression, argon beam coagulation, bipolar coagulation, radiofrequency, fibrin glue etc.

  • III. Large intraparenchymal hematomas. Intraoperative drainage and

hemostasis is mandatory.

  • IV. Large lacerations with transection of identifiable intrahepatic branches

of the hepatic artery, portal vein, hepatic vein or bile ducts, but amenable to suture repair. Pringle maneuver is necessary during surgery and the visible affected elements must be separately ligated. Ligation of the proper or common hepatic artery has been largely abandoned as is may lead to abscess formation.

  • V. Large lacerations with transection of identifiable intrahepatic branches

of the hepatic artery, portal vein, hepatic vein or bile ducts requiring resection of a portion of hepatic parenchyma.

  • VI. Large lacerations associated with injury of the retrohepatic veins and

vena cava resulting in massive hemorrhage. Due to progress in trauma care and fast transport these cases survive enough to be operated but surgical treatment require a trained team. Sometimes total vascular exclusion may be necessary to visualize and suture injuries to hepatic veins and VCI. To gain access to the suprahepatic VCI it is necessary to extend the midline incision into the mediastinum by splitting the sternum.

  • “U” sutures on parenchyma have been abandoned because of necrosis risk.

A correct mobilization of the liver may be necessary in order not to miss any lesion and to be able to gain access for a stable hemostasis. T- tubes (Kehr drainage) may be necessary in lesions of the common bile duct or if bilistasis is unperfect. Postoperative endoscopic sphincterotomy may be a substitute. If hemostasis is judged imperfect a correct packing of the liver may be the only solution.

  • Additional surgical procedures may be required due to intra- and extra-

abdominal injuries.

  • Stab wounds cause mainly minor injuries (Types I-III). Gunshots and

blunt trauma cause serious injuries (Types IV-VI) in half of these situations.

  • Preoperative assessment includes ultrasound, CT scan, puncture lavage.

The latter is faster and may be recommended in unstable patients, when CT may waste precious time. Laparoscopy is helpful but because of the large quantity of blood lesions may be difficult to localize and conversion must be decided.

  • Complications of liver trauma include abscesses, biliary fistulae,

hemobilia, liver failure, secondary bleeding, parenchymal necrosis.

  • Hemobilia is defined a bleeding draining in the biliary tree with

subsequent biliary colic, raised cholestasis enzymes and melena. Arteriography may be of help by detecting the source and obtaining hemostasis by selective embolisation.

THE HYDATID CYST

The hydatid cyst is a zoonotic infection caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus, causing cystic echinococcosis (CE).

Endemic countries are those were intermediate hosts are raised on a large scale outdoors (camels, pigs, sheep, cattle, goats, horses etc). The Balcans, Mediterranean countries, the Middle East, Argentina, Australia, New Zealand are among these endemic areas.Any person having had even a short stay in any of these can be at risk of being contaminated. This occurs by the ingestion of food, water or dirty hands contaminated by the eggs in the feces of a definitive host (dog, jackal or any other carnivore).

The adult tapeworm the definitive host eliminates its last segments, filled with eggs with the faeces of the carnivore. The eggs are ingested by the intermediate host (usually an herbivore). Under the influence of the alkaline intestinal juice they hatch into a hexacanth embryo, which, as its name suggests, has six (3 pairs) hooks used for penetration through the gut and from there in the veins. Having thus reached the portal system it penetrates the liver. About 2/3 of them remain in this first filter developing into a hepatic cyst. The rest of the embryos reach the heart and then pass into a second capillary filter, in the lungs, where they account for ¼ of the total localization. The parasites which managed to pass the lungs can affect then any organ, even bones or eyes.

Each larva can develop into a hydatid cyst which has an outer layer of inflammatory tissue and an inner germinal membrane that produces scolices and daughter cysts. When carnivores ingest the organs containing hydatid cysts of the intermediate host, the scolices of the daughter cysts are released in the small intestines and grow into adult worms, thus completing the life cycle of the worm.

The inflammatory tissue representing the external layer of the cyst is called pericyst does not really belong to the parasite and develops as a reaction of the host organ trying to limit the development of the cyst. The character of the pericyst depends on the host organ and varies with the age of the cyst. In the lung it tends to be much softer than in the liver. Older liver cysts have sometimes a partially calcified pericyst. Between the pericyst and the germinal membrane there is a white anhist membrane. The liquid produced by the germinal membrane is in noncomunicating cysts clear like “rock water”.The scolices grow like buds on the inner surface and then fall into the liquid and are called hydatid sand. The liquid contains parasitic proteins that will get in contact with the host in case of fissure of the cyst, causing an allergic reaction of variable scale.

The symptoms are caused by:

  • rupture of the cyst
  • infection of the cyst or affected organs
  • compression of any neighbouring organ. The rupture of the liver cyst can happen in:
  • biliary tree
  • free peritoneum
  • surrounding hollow viscus.

The erosion into the biliary tree can establish a small communication, with allergic symptoms - flushing, urticaria or a major rupture which can lead even to anaphylactic shock. Especially if a piece of membrane migrates into the biliary tree pain, chills and fever and jaundice will appear due to angiocolitis. Biliary obstruction can be caused by a late stenosis of the Oddi sphincter due to the irritating hydatid liquid. Depending on the affected organ the content of the cyst can be eliminated by vomit, stool, vomica or urine. Cysts close to the inferior surface of the liver can open in the free peritoneum with the long-term risk of hydatidosis (peritoneal seeding of the scolex, with multiple cysts developing)Cysts on the upper, convex surface or the liver can perforate the diafragm but, because of pleuro-pulmonary symphisis developingin that area, seldom open in the free pleural cavity.

The cysto-biliary fistula leads to the infection of the cavity, with symptoms of hepatic abscess.

The physical exam can find:

  • urticaria
  • jaundice
  • fever
  • asimetric hepatomegaly etc.

The parasite dies when infection occurs but also if the fibrosis of the pericyst stops its evolution. The fibrosis may evolve even in towards partial or total calcification.

Differentials

While weighing the differentials several steps must be taken. First the syndromes must be considered:

  • jaundice
  • persistent fever
  • hepatomegaly
  • allergic reaction.

The diagnose to be considered for the differentials are:

  • biliary obstruction
  • acute hepatitis
  • hepatic abscesses
  • hepatic nonparasitic cyst
  • Budd-Chiari Syndrome
  • Hepatic tumors, primary and metastatic

The lab studies may have following parameter changed:

  • elevated bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase, leukocytosis due to the

biliary obstruction

  • eosinophilia secondary to the allergic reaction.

The most reliable routine test is the ELISA with a sensitivity of 90% and even higher specificity.

Plain abdominal films are usually normal. Seldom a calcification of the pericysts may be observed.

Ultrasound is the best method for diagnose. The Gharbi classification is used for liver hydatid cysts:

  • type I- pure fluid similar to a simple cysts
  • type II - fluid collection with hydatid sand and a split-wall floating

membrane

  • type III - fluid collection with septa, daughter cysts, or a honeycomb

image

  • type IV - heterogeneous content
  • type V cysts - reflecting thick walls.

The same classification may be applied to computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. If no daughter cysts, hydatid sand or membranes (Garbi I )are observed the differential with a nonparasitic cysts is difficult.

CT rarely brings supplemental data in comparison with ultrasound. It seems to be useful to differentiate cystic lesions of the liver. MRI is not routinely used in the imaging of hydatid liver cyst.

The Casoni test, an intradermoreaction at hydatid antigen, was abandoned because of false positive and intense allergic reactions.

ERCP is more useful in biliary complicated cysts, as it is the method of choice for the diagnose and minimally invasive treatment (sphincterothomy and membrane extraction) of the cysto-biliary fistulae.

Treatment

The chemotherapy in CE as sole method has limited indications:

  • contraindications of surgery
  • large number of cysts
  • more than one organ affected

The contraindications derive from the toxicity of the drugs and are useless in complicated and dead cysts. Albendazole – is less toxic than mebendazole. The treatment has to cover a total 3-6 months, with intervals of 14 days every month. Every fortnight a complete blood count and liver enzymes have to be checked.

About 70% of the liver CE stop or decrease. The thinner pericyst in younger patients may account for better results than in older people.

PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration) is an interventional ultrasound guided technique. The CE is punctioned, the contents aspirated, scolicidal agent injected and reaspirated after 15 minutes. The cavity may be repeatedly washed in the same session and is left filled with isotonic saline solution. The presence of scolices in the aspirated liquid confirmes the parasitic character of the cyst. Perioperative benzimidazole profilaxy, though indispensable, lowers the risk of local seeding.

PAIR can be applied in some contraindications of surgery, but has to avoided in Gharbi IV and complicated, superficial (spillage and seeding risk) cysts.

Surgery is still indicated in most cases. The contraindications are multiple affected organs and general contraindications to surgical procedures. Calcified cysts are probably dead so the indication is questionable. Following the level of specific antibodies may be a helpful.

There are several types of surgery:

  • total pericystectomy
  • hepatic resection
  • cystectomy with partial pericystectomy

Total pericystectomy consists in removing the parasite together with the whole pericyst. Hemorrhage risks are higher but the postoperative outcome is shorter because the complications associated to the residual cavity (biliary fistulae, abscess) are eliminated.

The hepatic resection avoids the risk of seeding but may be too aggressive as it removes also healthy tissue. It may be applied in large cysts when only a small part of peripheral liver has to be sacrificed.

Cystectomy with partial pericystectomy removes the parasite with the area of pericyst that is superficial.

Marsupialisation, consisting in suturing the edges of the pericyst at the abdominal wall is an obsolete technique.

The main objectives of the surgical treatment are:

  • sterilization of the parasite by injecting a scolicidal substance
  • removal of the inactivated parasite
  • reduction of the residual cavity.

Scolicidal agents now in use are 15% hypertonic saline solution, chlorhexidine and 0.5% cetrimide solution. Absolute alcohol, formalin and hydrogen peroxide were abandoned, the first two having a very irritating action on the biliary tree, with sclerosing cholangitis as a late complication.

The identifying of the cyst may be sometimes difficult in laparoscopic approach. Intraoperative ultrasound may be useful. After the cyst is identified the most superficial part is surrounded with gauze pads. These are soaked with scolicidal agent. The agent is injected in the cyst and the content of the cyst is evacuated after 10-15 minutes using a suction device. Care must be taken to avoid any spillage. There are funnel shaped devices that are placed on the pericyst and avoid the secondary peritoneal seeding.

The cavity must be checked for cysto-biliary fistulae. The laparoscope is most useful because it allows a good intracystic vision. In case of jaundice and suspected obstruction by membranes the common bile duct may be explored. ERCP before surgery may avoid this by endoscopic sphincterothomy and endoscopic membrane evacuation .

The reduction of the residual cavity, if the case, must be obtained with pursestring sutures. In large cavities it is better to choose a resection than to use omentum to fill the cavity.

The routine drainage of the cavity is necessary because pressure inside the cavity is now smaller than the pressure inside the biliary tree. This means that after 2-3 days the discharge from the cavity will have a biliary content. If the total flow/day exceeds 500ml of bile the prospect of spontaneous closure is very remote and an endoscopic sphincterothomy is advisable.

PROPHILAXY

Humans are intermediate hosts so every link of the parasites chain of life can and has to be intercepted.

  • proper hands hygiene
  • correct food processing for humans
  • proper handling of herbivores viscera
  • dealing with the problem of rogue dogs
  • medical prophilaxy of echinococcosis in dogs
  • correct food processing for dogs. Prognosis mainly is good in most uncomplicated cases of CE.

Secondary seeding by spillage or rupture is not always followed by

hydatidosis if proper measures are immediately taken.

Echinococcus multilocularis, causes alveolar echinococcosis (AE). Fortunately it is rare with 0.03-1.2 cases per 100,000 inhabitants. Endemic areas are most countries of central Europe.

The adult stage of E multilocularis occurs in foxes (seldom other carnivores), as definitive host. The intermediate hosts are rodents. Exposure to wild berries contamined with faeces of a definitive host is the most frequent way of contamination for humans.

The liver is the primary site of infection and the symptomatology is that of cirrhosis or HCC, with the same complications and liver failure.

The progression can occur over weeks, months, or years.

Metastasis are possible but unfrequent.

In AE, the CT scan findings are sometimes indistinguishable from those of hepatocellular carcinoma

The mortality rate is 100% for untreated AE.

Liver resection with an adequate safety margin is the only real treatment in EA. Perioperative chemotherapy (2 years) is mandatory to avoid recurrency. In locally advanced cases liver transplantation may be a viable option. Recurrency on the graft and metastasis are favorised by immunosuppression. Reduction resection combined with long term (10 years) chemotherapy may be tried.

Palliative or symptomatic minimally invasive treatment may target esophageal varices bleeding or other complications.

If radical surgery is combined with chemotherapy 10 years survival can reach 90%.

The evaluation of the extent in liver tumors starts with ultrasound and is easier in HCC as lymph node metastasis is not so frequent.

In patients with metastasis (usually colorectal cancer) a local recurrence has to be excluded by colonoscopy and other organs involvement by CT. A chest x-ray may be helpful in detecting pulmonary metastasis but the attitude towards synchronous liver and lung metastasis does not exclude resective surgery on both organs.

CT volumetric analysis is necessary for assessment of an adequate residual liver. This must be correlated with the function, the Child-Pugh classification being widely used for cirrhosis. Under normal conditions 20% of residual volume is sufficient for survival and regeneration augments the volume after resection. If less residual parenchyma is expected a portal embolisation or ligation on the diseased part can be performed prior to surgery. In a few weeks the affected parenchyma will shrink while the rest will compensate by hypertrophy. Thus, after resection, there will be enough liver left to ensure survival.

Regarding the outcome in metastatic tumors, several negative predictive factors could be established:

- lymph node involvement

- multiple metastasis

- tumor > 5 cm

- if metachronous metastasis are diagnosed in less than a year

- CEA > 200ng/ml preoperatively

Regarding the resection of liver tumor(s) the idea is to spare parenchyma. Number, position and relation to major vessels must be accurately established by CT portography. This method is able to detect even smaller tumors. In experienced centers invasion in major hepatic elements or VCI is not a contraindication for surgery.

Laparoscopy is a valid method for staging liver tumors. The usual umbilical scope port must be placed on the anterior axillary line because it allows the best vision on segments VI and VII.

The laparoscopic ultrasound probe allows a thorough assessment of the liver. If doubts persist a PET scan can be discussed.

In experienced centers, perioperative mortality dropped from 20% 30 years ago to less than 5%.

Intraoperatively bleeding has been the major problem and biliary leaks and postoperative hemorrhage are still the main causes for morbidity. The fundamentals of hepatic resections start with the correct knowledge of the segmental anatomy of the liver. Wedge resections and non-anatomical resections (tumorectomies) have uncertain safe margins and can be applied in small tumors.

A correct resection must ensure a proper inflow and outflow, otherwise complications (bleeding, necrosis, hepatic failure) are unavoidable. Regarding the inflow control, the portal branch on the side to be resected can be disected in the extrahepatic course and ligated. The change in color of the parenchyma delineates the resection. For sectorial resections the correspondent branch can be ligated after the transection of the parenchyma covering it. This control of the intrahepatic pedicles can be achieved by dividing the parenchyma in selected areas.

In completion of the Pringle maneuver the vascular exclusion can be obtained by placing clamps on VCI above and below the liver. Vascular exclusion can be used to avoid bleeding from the hepatic veins. Another method to minimize this is to maintain a low CVP.

The duration of the Pringle maneuver must not exceed 40 minutes for a healthy liver, or less, according to the liver status. Another variant is to alternate a shorter clamping (10 min) with 1-2 minutes of declamping. Liver cell damage can be reduced in selected cases by local hipotermia (ice packing).

The transection of liver parenchyma can be obtained by finger fracture, Kelly clamp crushing, ultrasound aspirator (Cavitron), harmonic scalpels (ultrasound scissors), water jet dissectors. The modern technologies are valuable in transecting the cirrhotic parenchyma. The argon bean coagulator or the bicomponent fibrin glue can help in securing hemostasis on the raw liver surface.

Adjuvant regional chemotherapy consists in placing a catheter in the proper hepatic artery and by means of a special injecting chamber the chemotherapic mixture pressurized in a balloon (hepatic artery infusion pump) is infused.

Liver transplantation, recommended in primary liver tumors, is not an option for patients with secondary liver malignancies because the immunosuppressive treatment will lead to an explosion of metastasis.

PRIMARY HEPATIC CARCINOMA

The incidence of hepatorcarcinoma (HCC) increased the last 3 decades because of the high rates of infectious hepatitis B and C. HCC accounts for 80% of primitive hepatic cancer.

The etiology of HCC is similar to that of cirrhosis because up to 80% of patients diagnosed with HCC have a history of cirrhosis:

- alcohol (1/3 of HCC)

- hepatitis B virus

- hepatitis C virus (co-infection with HBV augments the risk of

HCC)

- hemochromatosis

- aflatoxin- produced by fungi growing on peanuts or other

improperly stored food

- Wilson’s disease

- tyrosinemia

- glycogen storage disease

The symptoms and signs are those of cirrhosis:

- hepatomegaly

- jaundice

- variceal bleeding

- flapping tremor and hepatic encephalopathy

- ascites

- weight loss to cachexia

- splenomegaly

- spider angiomata

- collateral venous circulation (esophageal varices, hemorrhoids,

caput medusae etc.)

Lab Studies:

- usual modified values in cirrhosis (hepatoprive, inflammatory,

cholestatic, cytolytic etc. sdr)

- alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) > 20 ng/ml; values >500ng/ml

characteristic for HCC

Imaging Studies:

The logical order to choose is: ultrasonography, CT scanning, or MRI ( best sensitivity). Tumoral invasion in a portal branch is specific for HCC.Angiography demonstrates a typical tumor blush and may visualize tumors under 1 cm. Biopsy caries the risk of tumoral seeding and, considering the cirrhotic liver, of bleeding. Histology may show a variable differentiation, from anaplastic to well differentiated tumors.

Medical care must be recommended considering certain criteria:

- size

- number

- location of tumors

- presence of cirrhosis

- patency of portal vein

- metastatic disease

HCC is a relatively chemotherapy-resistant tumor so systemic chemotherapy must use a combination chemotherapy to achieve acceptable response rates. Chemoimmunotherapy adds to chemotherapy immunomodulatory agents, such as interferon-alpha. Antiangiogenesis agents (bevacizumab), active by inhibiting the neovascular formation, typical for tumor growth, are recommended due to the vascular richness of HCC. Based on the same characteristic chemoembolization is another method of choice in HCC. The chemotherapeutic agent impregnated in cellulose or gelatin foam particles as a vehicle is injected in the hepatic artery (by selective angiography). It may be used also for local recurrence after resection.

In selected cases liver resection is possible. The operative risk must be considered by combining data on:

- class of cirrhosis

- comorbidities

- overall performance status.

One of the limits is given by the quality of the remaining cirrhotic parenchyma. Unfortunately HCC develops on a cirrhotic liver and is usually multicentric.

Fibrolamellar HCC has a better prognosis for survival after surgical resection.

Liver transplantation in HCC is advisable if the local extent is limited. When surgery is contraindicated tumor ablation can be of help.

CHOLANGIOCARCINOMA

Cholangiocarcinomas (CCCs) are malignancies of the biliary duct system, as a consequence can be located at any level (intrahepatic, perihilar, extrahepatic).

Perihilar tumors (also known as Klatskin tumors, 1965) are the most common.

METASTATIC TUMORS OF THE LIVER

Metastatic liver tumors outnumber by far the primitive ones. The explanation lies in the rich capillary circulation which acts as a filter. The most frequently encountered origins for liver metastasis are:

- melanoma

- pancreas

- colon and rectum.

Liver metastasis are usually multiple. The association with other metastatic sites is not a contraindication for surgical treatment any more.

Unfortunately not all yield acceptable results from the resectional point of vue. Colo-rectal metastasis, with the most encouraging outcome, provide a 40% 5-year survival rate in some instances.

Synchronous liver metastasis may be resected in a single procedure with the primary colo-rectal tumor if judged feasible. There are some arguments against this idea:

- it associates a septical and an aseptical procedure

- blood loss may impair with the anastomotic healing

- not all the surgeons performing colo-rectal surgery are proficient

in liver surgery.

The classical approach was to perform resection only if all metastasis could be remover. In selected cases the first hepatectomy is addressed to the most affected lobe. The remaining part may be treated with ablative procedures. After a short but necessary time for liver regeneration another resection can be performed on the remaining parenchyma.

Percutaneous ethanol or acetic acid injection as ablation techniques were practically abandoned in favor of other more efficient methods.

Cryoterapy, the oldest termic ablation technique, destroys tumors by freezing-thawing cycles. Cooper in 1913 was the first to use cryoterapy close to todays manner by developing a probe using liquid nitrogen, which was able to lower the temperature to -196˚C. Up to 4 or even more metastasis (if neuroendocrine) can be treated in one session, which can be repeated if necessary. The probe can be placed under direct vision, ultrasound guided or by laparoscopic approach. The probe for percutaneous approach can be as thin as 2,5mm. In order to ensure the destruction two cycles freezing-thawing must be completed. Specific complications are the cryogenic shock with multiorganic failure, bleeding due to the fracture of the frozen area and tumoral seeding.

Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) gained wide acceptance in tumor destruction. Developed in the late `80 it was intended for hemostasis but ended in being used for tumor ablation.

RFA uses a high frequency alternative current ( >300.000Hz) which raises the temperature of the tissues at values that coagulate protein with subsequent necrosis and tumor destruction. The current produces a very fast vibration of the ions in the tissue. The coagulated areas do not conduct the current thus limiting the extent of the destruction to maximum 3cm. The radius can be augmented to 5 cm if a flow of saline solution is passed though the electrodes’ orifices. The saline ensures the cooling and a better transmission of the current. The umbrella shaped probe has 9 electrodes in a bundle which deploys as an umbrella when the sheath is retracted. Thus the area of destruction has the shape of 9 added spheres, instead of only one.

Circulating blood has a cooling effect on the tissue so the destructive effect is weaker in the proximity of the larger hepatic vessels. Pringle maneuver and total vascular exclusion raise the temperature in the targeted area. Complications that may arise are: hemorrhage and hematoma, abscess, thrombosis, biliary duct stenosis etc.

The idea of combining several electrodes in line made possible the coagulation of a “slice” of tissue thus obtaining the hemostasis before the division of the parenchyma. Habib was the first to develop and use such a bipolar device with 4 (two each) electrodes 6 or 10 cm long. This device allows resections with a minimal blood loss even in cirrhotic patients and is tissue sparing.

Microwaves (2450 MHz) produce rotation and vibration of water molecules with heat production. The first type of electrodes where too large for percutaneous approach. Modern equipment consists in a generator and a monopolar needle- electrode which can be passed though a14 G needle. Each activation can destroy a sphere of 1,6cm. By focusing on a small area temperature raises enough to destroy tissue.

LIVER TRANSPLANTATION

The first liver transplantation with an acceptable survival (13 months) was communicated by Starzl in 1967. The indications are nowadays quite wide:

1. chronic liver diseases in advanced stages

2. primaryunresectable tumors limited to the liver

3. acute hepatitis with liver failure

4. transplant rejection.

Contraindications are:

1. compensated cirrhosis

2. extrahepatic malignancy

3. severe and uncontrolled extrahepatic infection

4. advanced cardiopulmonary disease

5. multisystem organ failure

6. active substance abuse

7. anatomic abnormalities that preclude performing the surgical

procedure of liver transplantation.

In addition to the traditional cadaveric liver transplantation several other variants meant to cover the shortage of donated cadaveric livers were developed. Much more demanding from the technical point of view, these techniques are applied in center experienced in microsurgery and standard liver transplantation.

Split-liver transplantation takes advantage of the knowledge gained in reduced-liver transplantation and increase the organ supply by using the right lobe or trisegmental graft that remains after the left lateral segment or left lobe is removed for a pediatric recipient.

The concept of living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) is based on the regenerative capacities of the human liver. LDLT began as a means for parents of children with severe liver disease to donate a portion of their healthy liver to replace their child's entire damaged liver. Because of the widespread shortage of cadaveric livers it began to be applied also in adults. Also in some countries the idea of cadaveric donors is not easily accepted. In LDLT a piece of healthy liver is surgically removed from a living person and transplanted into a recipient.

Domino liver transplantation, wherein a patient who himself undergoes liver transplantation in turn donates his liver to another recipient, has been performed since 1995. Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy livers are by far the most common source and recipients do not develop symptoms after domino liver transplantation. Domino recipients with nonmalignant indications for liver transplantation show excellent long-term survivals.
